small_guidance:
- The conv_transpose (now conv2d) dominates runtime; the fused tail kernel is already very cheap. Within the tail, try adding larger BLOCK_SIZE configs (32768) and a single-pass version when H_out*W_out ≤ BLOCK_SIZE to drop the loop overhead. Also test num_warps=2 since per-program work is small (one (n,c) pair, 16384 elements).
- Consider eliminating the `w_conv = w.transpose(0,1).flip([2,3]).contiguous()` allocation per forward call by caching it (invalidate if weight changes / training). This saves a memcpy on the hot path.
- For the conv2d call, try `channels_last` memory format for the input/weight — on Ada, cuDNN often picks a much faster kernel for 64-channel 256×256 inputs in NHWC.
large_guidance:
- Replace the F.conv2d with a custom Triton conv kernel that fuses the entire pipeline (conv → 2×2 maxpool → hardtanh → spatial mean → tanh) into one or two kernels. One program per (n, oc_tile, out_spatial_tile) computing conv via an implicit im2col GEMM, then immediately doing the 2×2 max-reduce and accumulating into a per-(n,c) sum register; final tanh in an epilogue. This avoids writing the [128,64,256,256]=2 GB conv output to HBM entirely, which is the real bottleneck.
- Since stride=1, padding=1, kernel=3, the conv output is the same spatial shape as input. Use a direct conv (not im2col GEMM) with channels_last layout: BLOCK tiles of (BLOCK_H=2, BLOCK_W=Wtile, BLOCK_OC=64), loop over IC in chunks of 16/32, accumulate 9 taps per IC. Fuse the 2×2 max immediately on the 2-row tile before storing/reducing.
- Two-stage design: stage-1 kernel writes pooled+hardtanh output [N,C,128,128] (4× smaller) while doing conv inline; stage-2 reduces to mean+tanh. This is simpler than full fusion and still eliminates the largest intermediate.
